lessons.title: Lists
lessons.objective: Make lists, read items by position and count them.

steps.text: A list keeps many values in order. len() counts them.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: Positions start at 0, so nums[0] is the first item: 4.

steps.text: Negative positions count from the end: -1 is the last item.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: Positions are 0, 1 and 2, so colours[2] is the third item: blue.

steps.text: The list has 3 items, so the last position is 2. Fix line 2.
steps.hint: Positions are 0, 1 and 2.
steps.explanation: There is no position 3 in a 3-item list (an IndexError). The last item is pets[2] or pets[-1].

steps.text: Make a list of the numbers 2, 4 and 6, then print how many items it has (3).
steps.hint: Put the numbers in [ ] and use len().

lessons.title: Changing lists
lessons.objective: Add, change and remove list items.

steps.text: append() adds an item to the end of a list.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: scores[0] = 9 replaces the first item.

steps.text: remove() takes away a value; pop() takes the last item and gives it back.
steps.code:
bag = ["pen", "book", "ruler"]
bag.remove("book")
print(bag)
last = bag.pop()
print(last)
print(bag)

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: append() added one item, so the list has 4.

steps.text: append needs brackets. Fix line 2.
steps.hint: Put the value inside append( ).
steps.explanation: Methods are called with brackets: team.append("Bala").

steps.text: Start with an empty list, append 10 and then 20, and print the list.
steps.hint: An empty list is [ ]. Then use append() twice.

lessons.title: Slices and loops
lessons.objective: Take part of a list and loop through every item.

steps.text: A slice [start:stop] takes the items from start up to, but not including, stop.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: [2:] starts at position 2 and goes to the end.

steps.text: for goes through every item in a list.
steps.code:
marks = [70, 85, 90]
total = 0
for m in marks:
    total = total + m
print(total)

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: The loop prints each word in capitals, one per line.

steps.text: A for line ends with a colon. Fix line 2.
steps.code:
names = ["Siti", "Wei"]
for n in names
    print(n)
steps.hint: Add : at the end of the line.
steps.explanation: Python needs a colon at the end of a for line.

steps.text: Print every number in [3, 6, 9] doubled, one per line.
steps.hint: Loop with for and print n * 2.

lessons.title: Tuples
lessons.objective: Use tuples for values that should not change.

steps.text: A tuple is like a list in round brackets, but it can't be changed.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: Position 1 is the second value: 128.

steps.text: You can unpack a tuple into separate variables.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: x is 4 and y is 9, so x + y is 13.

steps.text: Tuples can't be changed, so make a new one. Fix line 2.
steps.hint: Make a new tuple instead of changing one item.
steps.explanation: point[1] = 3 is a TypeError: tuples can't be changed. Make a new tuple instead.

steps.text: Unpack the tuple (7, 2) into a and b, then print a - b (5).
steps.hint: a, b = (7, 2) unpacks both values.

lessons.title: Stacks
lessons.objective: Use a list as a stack: last in, first out.

steps.text: A stack is like a pile of plates: add to the top and take from the top. append() pushes; pop() takes the top.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: pop() removes the last item: the top of the stack.

steps.text: The top of the stack is the last item: s[-1] looks at it without taking it.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: 8 was taken off the top, so 5 is on top now.

steps.text: Undo should take the newest action off the stack. Fix line 4.
steps.code:
actions = ["type", "draw"]
actions.append("erase")
print(actions)
undone = actions.pop(0)
print(undone)
steps.hint: pop() with no number takes the last item.
steps.explanation: pop(0) takes the oldest item; a stack takes from the top with pop().

steps.text: Push 1, 2 and 3 onto an empty stack, then pop once and print what came off (3).
steps.hint: Use append() three times, then print(s.pop()).

lessons.title: Queues
lessons.objective: Use a queue: first in, first out.

steps.text: A queue is like the line at the canteen: first in, first out. deque takes from the front quickly with popleft().
steps.code:
from collections import deque
line = deque(["Ali", "Mei"])
line.append("Raju")
print(line.popleft())
print(list(line))

steps.text: What will this print?
steps.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.popleft()
print(list(q))
steps.explanation: popleft() removes the first item.

steps.text: len() tells you how many are waiting.
steps.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append("A")
q.append("B")
print(len(q))

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque(["x", "y"])
q.append("z")
print(q.popleft())
steps.explanation: x joined the queue first, so it leaves first.

steps.text: A queue serves the person at the front. Fix line 3.
steps.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque(["Siti", "Wei", "Arun"])
first = q.pop()
print(first)
steps.hint: popleft() takes from the front.
steps.explanation: pop() takes from the back; a queue serves the front with popleft().

steps.text: Make a deque with 5 and 10, append 15, then popleft() and print what came out (5).
steps.solution:
from collections import deque
q = deque([5, 10])
q.append(15)
print(q.popleft())
steps.hint: from collections import deque, then deque([5, 10]).

lessons.title: Linear search
lessons.objective: Find an item by checking each one.

steps.text: Linear search checks the items one by one until it finds the target.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: index() does a linear search and gives the position: 2.

steps.text: A search function returns the position, or -1 when the target isn't there.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: "c" isn't in the list, so the loop ends and find returns -1.

steps.text: The search must compare with ==. Fix line 3.
steps.hint: == compares; = stores.
steps.explanation: An if needs a comparison: items[i] == target.

lessons.title: Binary search
lessons.objective: Search a sorted list by halving it.

steps.text: In a sorted list you can check the middle and throw away half each time. That is binary search.
// divides and drops the remainder. What is the middle position?
steps.explanation: 9 // 2 is 4: the remainder is dropped.

steps.text: Each check halves what is left: 1000 items shrink to 1 in just 9 halvings.
steps.code:
n = 1000
checks = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    checks = checks + 1
print(checks)

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: mid is 2, and nums[2] is 5.

steps.text: When the middle is too small, search the right half. Fix line 9.
steps.hint: Move low up past mid.
steps.explanation: If the middle is too small, the target is to the right: low = mid + 1.

steps.text: Print the middle position of a 7-item list, from 0 to 6, using // (3).

lessons.title: Sorting
lessons.objective: Sort lists with sorted() and sort().

steps.text: sorted() gives a new sorted list; reverse=True sorts from the biggest.
What will this print?
steps.explanation: Text sorts in alphabetical order.

steps.text: list.sort() sorts the list itself; key=len sorts by length.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: After sorting, the smallest number is first.

steps.text: sort() changes the list and gives back None. Fix line 2.
steps.hint: Call nums.sort() on its own line.
steps.explanation: nums.sort() returns None, so nums = nums.sort() loses the list.

steps.text: Print the list [5, 2, 8] sorted from biggest to smallest.
steps.hint: sorted(..., reverse=True)

lessons.title: Bubble sort
lessons.objective: See how a sorting algorithm swaps neighbours.

steps.text: Bubble sort compares neighbours and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. Big values bubble to the end.
Python can swap two values in one line. What will this print?
steps.code:
a, b = 3, 7
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
steps.explanation: a, b = b, a swaps the two values.

steps.text: One pass moves the biggest value to the end.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.code:
nums = [2, 1]
if nums[0] > nums[1]:
    nums[0], nums[1] = nums[1], nums[0]
print(nums)
steps.explanation: 2 is bigger than 1, so they swap.

steps.text: To sort from smallest, swap when the left one is bigger. Fix line 4.
steps.hint: Swap when the left one is bigger: >.
steps.explanation: Swapping when nums[j] > nums[j + 1] sorts from smallest to biggest.

steps.text: Start with a, b = 1, 2. Swap them so print(a, b) shows 2 1.
steps.solution:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
steps.hint: a, b = b, a swaps them.
